claims.text: The initial material is a conventionally cast CoCrFeMnNi Cantor alloy.
The initial alloy is a single-phase, disordered, homogeneous solid solution.
Directed solidification of the melt will induce segregation into copper-rich nanolamellae.
Annealing at 700–800°C under an inert atmosphere will optimize and stabilize the nanolamellar morphology.
The resulting mediator will consist of uniformly distributed copper-rich nanolamellae embedded in the HEA matrix.
The copper-rich nanolamellae will be coherent with the HEA matrix.
Copper-rich nanolamellae will create continuous, highly conductive pathways through the alloy.
The embedded conductive pathways will enhance heat transfer.
Coherent copper/HEA interfaces will preserve overall mechanical strength.
Coherent copper/HEA interfaces will preserve microstructural stability.
The processed alloy will have approximately 20–30% greater thermal conductivity than the baseline Cantor alloy.
The conductivity improvement will occur without sacrificing mechanical robustness.
The processed alloy will retain stable high-temperature behavior.
The claimed benefits will persist during cyclic thermal loading between room temperature and 900°C.
The claimed benefits will persist under mechanical loads typical of reactor intermediate materials.
Prior literature and preliminary observations support the ability of copper segregation to form conductive pathways.

contradictions.description: The stated starting alloy contains only Co, Cr, Fe, Mn, and Ni, and the intervention adds no copper. Directed solidification and annealing therefore cannot produce copper-rich nanolamellae by segregation from the specified material.

The hypothesis attributes nanolamella formation to directed solidification, whereas the intervention additionally requires a separate annealing operation; thus the proposed intervention is not strictly a single processing action.
